newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF official arrives in Pakistan for loan talks.
newsitem.headline: IMF official arrives in Pakistan for loan talks.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official arrived in Islamabad on Wednesday to try to complete talks with Pakistan's caretaker government on resumption of a $600 million standby loan, an official said.
The official at the Finance Ministry said that Paul Chabrier, head of the IMF's Middle East department, would meet Pakistani officials later in the day.

Chabrier had been expected to fly to Islamabad on November 5, but postponed his trip after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government the same day, citing corruption, misrule and extrajudicial killings.
Leghari installed Meraj Khalid to head an interim government to lead Pakistan into a general election on February 3.

The IMF withheld the June and September tranches of the standby loan, worth about $80 million each, because it was unhappy with the economic performance of Bhutto's government and its budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).

Shahid Javed Burki, who has taken a 90-day leave of absence from his job as a World Bank vice-president to head the Finance Ministry in the interim government, said on Saturday that he hoped Pakistan would now gain greater access to IMF funds.
Government officials have indicated that they would like to strengthen a Letter of Intent drawn up by the Bhutto government to secure expanded IMF lending, but have given no details.
Burki, named adviser to the prime minister on finance and economic affairs, has outlined a sweeping programme to shore up Pakistan's shaky economy and regain the favour of the IMF.

Pakistan had to turn to the IMF for a standby loan after a financial crisis in October 1995. But the economy continued to deteriorate, with a widening current account deficit, shrinking foreign reserves and a budget deficit spinning out of control.

The caretaker government says the 1995/96 budget deficit reached 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, well above the revised figure of 5.8 percent acknowledged by Bhutto's economic team, which had originally given a figure of 5.0 percent.
Officials say the IMF is demanding that the budget gap be reduced to 4.0 percent of GDP in 1996/97.
